source_text: καίων εἰς σωτηρίαν· ὁποῖοί τινες γεγόνασιν Ὑμέναιός τε καὶ Ἀλέξανδρος, οἰόμενοί τε καὶ λέγοντες ἀνάστασιν ἤδη γεγονέναι. Καὶ προστεθεῖεν ἂν τούτοις, οἱ ἀπονεύοντες ἀχαλίνως πρὸς πᾶν ὁτιοῦν τῶν ἐκτόπων, καὶ τῆς ἑαυτῶν διανοίας τὸν καρπὸν παραῤῥιπτοῦντες ἁπλῶς εἰς ἑώλους καὶ ἀσελγεῖς ἡδονάς. Οὐκοῦν ὁ λεπρὸς μὲν καὶ γονοῤῥυὴς, τοῦτ' ἔστιν, ὁ τοῖς νεκρότητος ἔργοις ἐνισχημένος (εἶεν δ' ἂν ἔργα νεκρότητος, τὰ τῆς σαρκὸς πάθη), καὶ ὁ τὴν ἔσω καρποφορίαν, τὴν εἰς νοῦν δηλονότι καὶ κεκρυμμένην, οὐκ ἀπαράφθορον ἔχων, ἀποχωρείτω, φησὶ, τῶν ἁγίων, ἕως ἂν καθαρισθῇ. Ὡς γὰρ ὁ θεσπέσιος ἔφη Παῦλος, «Ὃς ἂν ἐσθίῃ τὸ σῶμα τοῦ Κυρίου καὶ πίνῃ τὸ ποτήριον αὐτοῦ ἀναξίως, κρῖμα ἑαυτῷ ἐσθίει καὶ πίνει, μὴ διακρίνων τὸ σῶμα αὐτοῦ. Δοκιμαζέτω δὲ,» φησὶν, «ἄνθρωπος ἑαυτὸν, καὶ τότε ἐκ τοῦ ἄρτου ἐσθιέτω, καὶ ἐκ τοῦ ποτηρίου πινέτω.» {ΠΑΛΛ.} Ἄριστα ἔφης. {ΚΥΡ.} Ἄθρει δὴ οὖν, ὦ Παλλάδιε, τὸ ἀκριβὲς τοῦ νόμου· κεχώρηκε γὰρ ἥκιστά γε κατὰ μόνων τοῦ λεπροῦ καὶ γονοῤῥυοῦς, συγκαταδικάζει δὲ ὥσπερ αὐτοῖς, καὶ εἴ τις ἅψαιτο τυχὸν τῶν ἠῤῥωστηκότων, λεπροῦ δὴ λέγω καὶ γονοῤῥυοῦς. «Καὶ ὁ ἁπτόμενος,» φησὶ, «πάσης ἀκαθαρσίας ψυχῆς, ἢ ᾧ ἂν ἐξέλθῃ κοίτη σπέρματος αὐτοῦ, ἀκάθαρτος ἔσται.» {ΠΑΛΛ.} Καὶ τίς ἂν γένοιτο τοῖς ἐπαφωμένοις ἡ ἀπό γε τούτου ζημία; {ΚΥΡ.} Οὐδεμία μὲν, κατά γε τὸν ἐν προχείρῳ λόγον. Καταμιανεῖ γὰρ οὐχὶ τὴν ἀνθρώπου ψυχὴν, σώματος ἐπαφή. Πνευματικὸς δὲ ὁ νόμος, καὶ διδάσκει πάλιν ἡμᾶς αἰνιγματωδῶς, ὡς ἀκάθαρτοι μὲν ἐν ἐγκλήμασι μολυσμῶν, οἱ ψυχικοῖς ἔνοχοι πάθεσιν. Συγκαταμιαίνονται δὲ αὐτοῖς καὶ οἱ θιγγάνοντες, ἤτοι κολλώμενοι, κατὰ σχέσιν δὲ δηλονότι τῆς ταυτοβουλίας, ἤγουν ταυτοεργίας· «Φθείρουσι γὰρ ἤθη χρηστὰ ὁμιλίαι κακαί·» καὶ, «Μερὶς μὲν οὐδεμία πιστῷ μετὰ ἀπίστου·» πολέμιον δὲ καὶ ἀσύμβατον τῷ σκότῳ τὸ φῶς. Καὶ ἀληθὲς, ὅτι «Μετὰ ὁσίου ὁσιωθήσῃ, καὶ μετὰ ἀνδρὸς ἀθώου ἀθῶος ἔσῃ, καὶ μετὰ ἐκλεκτοῦ ἐκλεκτὸς ἔσῃ, καὶ μετὰ στρεβλοῦ διαστρέψεις.» Ὅτι δὲ οὐχὶ τὸ ἀῤῥωστῆσαι μόνον τὰ ἐκτοπώτατα τῶν παθῶν, μόνοις ἔσται τοῖς ἠῤῥωστηκόσι παγχάλεπον, ἀλλὰ καὶ οἵπερ ἂν γένοιντο σύμφρονές τε καὶ ὁμογνώμονες, οὐ μείοσιν ἢ ἐκεῖνοι καταμιανθήσονται μολυσμοῖς, παρέδειξεν εὐθὺς ἐπειπὼν, ὅτι «Ὅστις ἐὰν ἅψηται παντὸς ἑρπετοῦ ἀκαθάρτου, μιανεῖ αὐτὸν, ἢ ἐπ' ἀνθρώπῳ ἐν ᾧ μιανεῖ κατὰ πᾶσαν ἀκαθαρσίαν αὐτοῦ, ψυχὴ ἥτις ἂν ἅψηται αὐτῶν, ἀκάθαρτος ἔσται ἕως ἑσπέρας.» Ἑρπετὰ δὲ πικρὰ καὶ ἰοβόλα λέγεσθαί τε καὶ εἶναί φαμεν, τοὺς οἷσπερ ἂν εἴη πρέπων ὁ λόγος, «Ἰὸς ἀσπίδων ὑπὸ τὰ χείλη αὐτῶν· ὧν τὸ στόμα ἀρᾶς καὶ πικρίας γέμει.» Εἶεν δ' ἂν οὗτοι καὶ πρό γε τῶν ἄλλων οἱ τὰ ὀρθὰ διαστρέφοντες, καὶ τοῖς ἁπλουστέροις τὸν ὀλέθρου πρόξενον ἐνηχοῦντες λόγον, ἀποφέροντές γε πρὸς ἐννοίας οὐκ ἀγαθὰς, καὶ εἰς δόξαν ἐπὶ Θεῷ τὴν δι
pass_a_gloss: [unable to understand nothing of the things neces]sary for salvation; such have been Hymenaeus and Alexander, both thinking and saying that the resurrection has already happened. And there might be added to these those who turn aside unbridled to any one whatever of the outlandish things, and simply throw away the fruit of their own understanding into stale and wanton pleasures. So the leper and the one with a flux, that is, the one held fast by the works of deadness (and the works of deadness would be the passions of the flesh), and the one not having uncorrupted the inner fruit-bearing, clearly the one in the mind and hidden, let him withdraw, he says, from the holy things until he is cleansed. For as the inspired Paul said, 'Whoever eats the body of the Lord and drinks his cup unworthily eats and drinks judgment to himself, not discerning his body. But let a man,' he says, 'test himself, and then eat from the bread and drink from the cup.' PALL.: You spoke excellently. CYR.: Observe then, Palladius, the exactness of the law; for it has gone not at all against the leper and the one with a flux alone, but condemns together with them, as it were, also anyone who perhaps touches the sick, I mean the leper and the one with a flux. 'And the one touching,' he says, 'any uncleanness of a soul, or from whom a bed of his seed goes out, shall be unclean.' PALL.: And what loss could come to those touching from this? CYR.: None, according to the ready meaning. For the touch of a body will not defile the soul of a man. But the law is spiritual, and teaches us again in riddles that unclean in charges of defilements are those liable to passions of the soul. And defiled together with them are also those handling, that is, clinging, clearly by relation of sameness of will, or sameness of work. For 'bad companionships corrupt good habits'; and 'no portion for a believer with an unbeliever'; and hostile and irreconcilable to the darkness is the light. And true is it that 'with the holy you will be made holy, and with an innocent man you will be innocent, and with the chosen you will be chosen, and with the crooked you will turn aside.' And that not only to be sick with the most outlandish of the passions will be very hard for the sick alone, but those too who become of one mind and one judgment will be defiled with no lesser defilements than they, he showed at once, saying after: 'Whoever touches any unclean creeping thing, it will defile him, or upon a man in whom it will defile according to all his uncleanness, a soul which touches them shall be unclean until evening.' Creeping things bitter and venom-casting we say are both called and are those for whom this word would be fitting: 'The venom of asps under their lips; whose mouth is full of curse and bitterness.' And these would be, before the others, those who distort the right things, and sound into the simpler the word that brings about ruin, carrying them off to thoughts not good, and to an opinion about God that is dis[torted]
pass_b_english: Cyril: …necessary for salvation. Such were Hymenaeus and Alexander (1 Timothy 1:20), who both thought and said that the resurrection had already taken place (2 Timothy 2:17–18). To these may be added those who turn without restraint toward every kind of outrage, and simply throw away the fruit of their own minds on stale and wanton pleasures. So the leper and the man with a discharge, that is, the one held fast by the works of deadness (and the works of deadness would be the passions of the flesh), and the one who does not keep his inner fruitfulness uncorrupted, the hidden fruitfulness of the mind, must withdraw, he says, from the holy things until he is cleansed (Leviticus 22:4). For as the inspired Paul said, ‘Whoever eats the body of the Lord and drinks his cup unworthily eats and drinks judgment on himself, not discerning his body’ (1 Corinthians 11:27, 29). ‘But let a man,’ he says, ‘examine himself, and then let him eat of the bread and drink of the cup’ (1 Corinthians 11:28).

Cyril: Notice, then, Palladius, how precise the law is. It does not stop at the leper and the man with a discharge alone, but condemns along with them, as it were, anyone who happens to touch those who are sick, I mean the leper and the man with a discharge. ‘And whoever touches,’ he says, ‘anything unclean from a person, or one from whom an emission of semen goes out, shall be unclean’ (Leviticus 22:4).
Palladius: And what harm could come from this to those who touch them?

Cyril: None at all, if we take the words at face value, for a touch of the body will not defile a person’s soul. But the law is spiritual (Romans 7:14), and once again it teaches us in figures that those who are guilty of the passions of the soul are unclean, charged with defilement; and those who touch them, or cling to them, are defiled together with them, clearly by the bond of a shared will or shared deeds. For ‘bad company ruins good character’ (1 Corinthians 15:33), and ‘a believer has no share with an unbeliever’ (2 Corinthians 6:15), and light is hostile to darkness and can make no terms with it (2 Corinthians 6:14). It is true, too, that ‘with the holy you will be made holy, and with the innocent man you will be innocent, and with the chosen you will be chosen, and with the crooked you will turn crooked’ (Psalm 18:25–26). He showed at once that to be sick with the most outrageous of the passions will be grievous not for the sick alone, but that those who come to share their mind and judgment will be defiled with stains no less than theirs, for he added: ‘Whoever touches any unclean creeping thing, it will defile him, or a man through whom he will be defiled by any of his uncleanness; the soul that touches them shall be unclean until evening’ (Leviticus 22:5–6). We say that the bitter and venomous creeping things, in name and in fact, are those whom this saying would fit: ‘The poison of asps is under their lips; their mouth is full of cursing and bitterness’ (Romans 3:13–14). And these would be, before all others, those who twist what is right and drum into simpler people a teaching that leads to ruin, carrying them off to thoughts that are not good and to a twisted opinion about God…

choices.why: Leviticus 22:4 πάσης ἀκαθαρσίας ψυχῆς: in the Hebrew this is corpse-uncleanness; Cyril reads ψυχή as 'a person' and applies it to touching the leper and the man with a discharge, so the English keeps 'anything unclean from a person'.

anf_compare.notes: No public-domain English of Cyril De adoratione Book 12 exists. Translated fresh from the PG 68 Greek on 2026-10-23; the earlier English of this book was not used as a base.

apparatus.note: PG OCR; column may cut mid-sentence.

Opens mid-word: §8 ends ἀναγ-, §9 begins -καίων εἰς σωτηρίαν, so the first turn starts '…necessary for salvation'. Hymenaeus and Alexander are paired in 1 Timothy 1:20, but the saying that the resurrection has already happened belongs to Hymenaeus and Philetus in 2 Timothy 2:17–18; Cyril merges the two, and both are cited. 'Until he is cleansed' is Leviticus 22:4 (ἕως ἂν καθαρισθῇ). The Pauline quotation is a free blend: 'the body of the Lord' and 'his cup' are Cyril's wording, the clause 'eats and drinks judgment… not discerning the body' is 11:29, the 'unworthily' frame is 11:27; 11:28 follows. Leviticus 22:4 πάσης ἀκαθαρσίας ψυχῆς: in the Hebrew this is corpse-uncleanness; Cyril reads ψυχή as 'a person' and applies it to touching the leper and the man with a discharge, so the English keeps 'anything unclean from a person'. Psalm 17:26–27 LXX = Psalm 18:25–26 English (also 2 Samuel 22:26–27); Cyril's ὁσιωθήσῃ ('you will be made holy') is kept. 'Light is hostile to darkness' is a paraphrase of 2 Corinthians 6:14, cited. 'The poison of asps… cursing and bitterness' follows Romans 3:13–14 word for word (itself from Psalm 140:3 = LXX 139:4 and Psalm 10:7 = LXX 9:28). 'Works of deadness' may echo the 'dead works' of Hebrews 6:1/9:14; too loose to cite. The last phrase δόξαν… τὴν δι|εστραμμένην is split across §9/§10; the whole phrase ('a distorted opinion about God') is rendered here and §10 opens with the next clause.

Drafted Pass A, kept as written (rewritten as a literal English gloss from the Greek in pass_a_gloss): [ἀναγ]καίων εἰς σωτηρίαν: (things) necessary for salvation. Such (ὁποῖοι) were Hymenaeus and Alexander, οἰόμενοι καὶ λέγοντες ἀνάστασιν ἤδη γεγονέναι. Added (προστεθεῖεν) to them: those ἀπονεύοντες ἀχαλίνως (unbridled) toward any of τὰ ἔκτοπα (outlandish/monstrous things), and παραρριπτοῦντες the καρπός of their διάνοια into ἑώλους (stale) and ἀσελγεῖς ἡδονάς. So the λεπρός and γονορρυής = the one ἐνισχημένος (held) in ἔργα νεκρότητος (glossed: τὰ τῆς σαρκὸς πάθη) and the one not having the inner καρποφορία (of νοῦς, κεκρυμμένη) ἀπαράφθορος (uncorrupted): ἀποχωρείτω τῶν ἁγίων ἕως ἂν καθαρισθῇ. Paul (θεσπέσιος): whoever eats the σῶμα of the Lord and drinks his ποτήριον ἀναξίως eats and drinks κρῖμα for himself, μὴ διακρίνων the body; δοκιμαζέτω ἄνθρωπος ἑαυτόν, then eat of the bread, drink of the cup. PALL: ἄριστα ἔφης. CYR: ἄθρει τὸ ἀκριβὲς τοῦ νόμου; it went (κεχώρηκε) not only against leper and flux-sufferer, but συγκαταδικάζει anyone who touches (ἅψαιτο) the sick. Quote: ὁ ἁπτόμενος πάσης ἀκαθαρσίας ψυχῆς, ἢ ᾧ ἂν ἐξέλθῃ κοίτη σπέρματος, ἀκάθαρτος ἔσται. PALL: what ζημία to those touching? CYR: none, κατὰ τὸν ἐν προχείρῳ λόγον (surface sense): σώματος ἐπαφή does not defile ψυχή. But νόμος πνευματικός, teaches αἰνιγματωδῶς: unclean ἐν ἐγκλήμασι μολυσμῶν are those ἔνοχοι ψυχικοῖς πάθεσιν; συγκαταμιαίνονται those θιγγάνοντες ἤτοι κολλώμενοι, κατὰ σχέσιν ταυτοβουλίας ἤγουν ταυτοεργίας (same will, same work). Quotes: φθείρουσιν ἤθη χρηστὰ ὁμιλίαι κακαί; μερὶς οὐδεμία πιστῷ μετὰ ἀπίστου; light is πολέμιον καὶ ἀσύμβατον to darkness; μετὰ ὁσίου ὁσιωθήσῃ, μετὰ ἀνδρὸς ἀθῴου ἀθῷος, μετὰ ἐκλεκτοῦ ἐκλεκτός, μετὰ στρεβλοῦ διαστρέψεις. That not only to be sick (ἀρρωστῆσαι) with τὰ ἐκτοπώτατα of the passions is παγχάλεπον for the sick alone, but σύμφρονες καὶ ὁμογνώμονες will be defiled οὐ μείοσι μολυσμοῖς, he showed (παρέδειξεν) by adding: whoever touches any ἑρπετὸν ἀκάθαρτον, μιανεῖ αὐτόν, or a man ἐν ᾧ μιανεῖ by all his uncleanness, ψυχὴ that touches them ἀκάθαρτος ἕως ἑσπέρας. Ἑρπετὰ πικρὰ καὶ ἰοβόλα (venomous) = those to whom fits: ἰὸς ἀσπίδων ὑπὸ τὰ χείλη, στόμα ἀρᾶς καὶ πικρίας γέμει. Above all: οἱ τὰ ὀρθὰ διαστρέφοντες, ἐνηχοῦντες (dinning) into τοῖς ἁπλουστέροις a λόγος ὀλέθρου πρόξενος, ἀποφέροντες to ἐννοίας οὐκ ἀγαθάς and εἰς δόξαν ἐπὶ Θεῷ τὴν δι[εστραμμένην] (word completed at the start of §10).
